subject: c12-phy
scope: CBSE Class XII Physics (042) 2026–27 written/theory Board-exam preparation; practical/internal-assessment material excluded.

weightage.label: Current Electricity + Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism (Ch 3–5)
Electromagnetic Induction, Alternating Currents, Electromagnetic Waves + Optics (Ch 6–10)
Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter + Atoms and Nuclei (Ch 11–13)

note: Official CBSE 2026-27 theory grouping: Electrostatics 16, Current Electricity + Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism 17, Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Currents + Electromagnetic Waves + Optics 18, Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter + Atoms and Nuclei 12, Electronic Devices 7; total 70.

reference.label: Electric Charges and Fields — Tip 1
reference.text: Draw the field direction before substituting values; electric field is a vector.

reference.label: Electric Charges and Fields — Tip 2
reference.text: Use superposition for multiple charges and keep signs/directions separate from magnitudes.

reference.label: Electric Charges and Fields — Tip 3
reference.text: For Gauss-law questions, first identify the symmetry before choosing a Gaussian surface.

reference.label: Electric Charges and Fields — Tip 4
reference.text: Distinguish electric flux from electric field; flux depends on field, area and angle.

reference.label: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance — Tip 1
reference.text: Potential is scalar, so add contributions algebraically.

reference.label: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance — Tip 2
reference.text: Keep the sign convention consistent when relating potential, work and potential energy.

reference.label: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance — Tip 3
reference.text: For capacitor combinations, decide series/parallel from the circuit connections before calculating equivalent capacitance.

reference.label: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance — Tip 4
reference.text: When a dielectric is inserted, identify whether the capacitor remains connected to the battery before deciding which quantities stay fixed.

reference.label: Current Electricity — Tip 1
reference.text: Convert the circuit into a clear diagram before applying Kirchhoff's rules.

reference.label: Current Electricity — Tip 2
reference.text: Keep current directions consistent; a negative solved current simply indicates the assumed direction was opposite.

reference.label: Current Electricity — Tip 3
reference.text: Separate emf and terminal voltage when internal resistance is present.

reference.label: Current Electricity — Tip 4
reference.text: For bridge problems, check the balance condition before doing unnecessary calculations.

reference.label: Moving Charges and Magnetism — Tip 1
reference.text: Use the right-hand rule carefully for magnetic-field and force directions.

reference.label: Moving Charges and Magnetism — Tip 2
reference.text: For a charged particle in a magnetic field, identify whether velocity is perpendicular, parallel or at an angle to B.

reference.label: Moving Charges and Magnetism — Tip 3
reference.text: Keep radius, angular frequency and time period relations connected when solving circular-motion questions.

reference.label: Moving Charges and Magnetism — Tip 4
reference.text: In galvanometer conversions, distinguish the required shunt resistance for an ammeter from the series resistance for a voltmeter.

reference.label: Magnetism and Matter — Tip 1
reference.text: Keep B, H, M and magnetic susceptibility conceptually distinct.

reference.label: Magnetism and Matter — Tip 2
reference.text: State the material type when discussing dia-, para- or ferromagnetism.

reference.label: Magnetism and Matter — Tip 3
reference.text: Use the direction of magnetisation and applied field carefully in conceptual questions.

reference.label: Magnetism and Matter — Tip 4
reference.text: Do not confuse magnetic dipole moment with magnetisation; magnetisation is moment per unit volume.

reference.label: Electromagnetic Induction — Tip 1
reference.text: Apply Lenz's law to determine the direction of induced current before using Faraday's law.

reference.label: Electromagnetic Induction — Tip 2
reference.text: Flux changes can come from changing B, area or orientation; identify what is changing.

reference.label: Electromagnetic Induction — Tip 3
reference.text: Keep self-induction and mutual induction conceptually separate.

reference.label: Electromagnetic Induction — Tip 4
reference.text: Check the sign of induced emf rather than using only its magnitude when direction is asked.

reference.label: Alternating Current — Tip 1
reference.text: Convert peak values to RMS values only when the question requires effective values.

reference.label: Alternating Current — Tip 2
reference.text: Compare XL and XC before deciding whether the circuit is net inductive or capacitive.

reference.label: Alternating Current — Tip 3
reference.text: At resonance, XL=XC; then simplify the impedance and power-factor relations.

reference.label: Alternating Current — Tip 4
reference.text: Track phase angle carefully; do not confuse current's phase with voltage's phase.

reference.label: Electromagnetic Waves — Tip 1
reference.text: Focus on the properties, production and uses of electromagnetic waves rather than inventing unnecessary numerical formulas.

reference.label: Electromagnetic Waves — Tip 2
reference.text: Remember that electromagnetic waves are transverse and do not require a material medium.

reference.label: Electromagnetic Waves — Tip 3
reference.text: Keep the order of the electromagnetic spectrum and typical applications clear.

reference.label: Electromagnetic Waves — Tip 4
reference.text: Distinguish displacement current and electromagnetic-wave concepts when answering conceptual questions.

reference.label: Ray Optics and Optical Instruments — Tip 1
reference.text: Draw a ray diagram before applying the mirror or lens formula.

reference.label: Ray Optics and Optical Instruments — Tip 2
reference.text: Use the CBSE Cartesian sign convention consistently for u, v, f and heights.

reference.label: Ray Optics and Optical Instruments — Tip 3
reference.text: Check whether the question asks for magnification, image nature, position or power before choosing the relation.

reference.label: Ray Optics and Optical Instruments — Tip 4
reference.text: For prism questions, identify the minimum-deviation condition before substituting.

reference.label: Wave Optics — Tip 1
reference.text: Draw the Young's double-slit geometry before using fringe-width relations.

reference.label: Wave Optics — Tip 2
reference.text: Distinguish path difference from fringe position.

reference.label: Wave Optics — Tip 3
reference.text: Use constructive and destructive interference conditions with the correct integer form.

reference.label: Wave Optics — Tip 4
reference.text: Keep wavelength, slit separation and screen distance in consistent units.

reference.label: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter — Tip 1
reference.text: Separate photon energy, work function and maximum kinetic energy in photoelectric-effect questions.

reference.label: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter — Tip 2
reference.text: Remember that intensity mainly affects photoelectric current, while frequency determines photon energy and threshold behaviour.

reference.label: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter — Tip 3
reference.text: Use stopping potential as an energy relation, not as a direct velocity formula.

reference.label: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter — Tip 4
reference.text: For de Broglie questions, identify whether momentum is given directly or must be obtained from kinetic energy.

reference.label: Atoms — Tip 1
reference.text: Keep Bohr's postulates and the hydrogen-like atom formulae connected.

reference.label: Atoms — Tip 2
reference.text: Check the principal quantum number n and nuclear charge Z before substituting.

reference.label: Atoms — Tip 3
reference.text: Energy levels are negative for bound states; be careful with signs when calculating transitions.

reference.label: Atoms — Tip 4
reference.text: Use the correct hydrogen-like assumption when applying the simple Bohr relations.

reference.label: Nuclei — Tip 1
reference.text: Distinguish mass defect, binding energy and binding energy per nucleon.

reference.label: Nuclei — Tip 2
reference.text: Keep atomic mass and nuclear mass conventions consistent in numerical problems.

reference.label: Nuclei — Tip 3
reference.text: Use 931.5 MeV per atomic mass unit when converting mass defect in u to energy in MeV.

reference.label: Nuclei — Tip 4
reference.text: For nuclear-reaction questions, check conservation of charge and nucleon number.

reference.label: Semiconductor Electronics — Tip 1
reference.text: Identify whether the question concerns intrinsic/extrinsic semiconductors, p-n junctions or a diode application.

reference.label: Semiconductor Electronics — Tip 2
reference.text: Keep forward bias and reverse bias conditions distinct.

reference.label: Semiconductor Electronics — Tip 3
reference.text: Draw the relevant circuit or characteristic when the question involves a diode or rectifier.

reference.label: Semiconductor Electronics — Tip 4
reference.text: Do not mix semiconductor-device terminology with the earlier electromagnetic chapters.

mistakes: Using a formula without checking its physical conditions or assumptions.
Skipping the diagram in field, circuit, ray-optics and wave-optics questions.
Confusing vector direction with scalar magnitude.
Not writing the final answer with the correct SI unit.
order: Start with Electrostatics (16 marks): Electric Charges and Fields → Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance.
Then Current Electricity and Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism (17 marks): Current Electricity → Moving Charges and Magnetism → Magnetism and Matter.
Then Electromagnetic Induction, Alternating Currents, Electromagnetic Waves and Optics (18 marks).
Then Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter, Atoms and Nuclei (12 marks).
Finish Electronic Devices (7 marks), then revise mixed numerical, derivation, diagram and conceptual questions.
